results.quote: Theorem 1.5. Let T be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of (T,w) in time O(n log h), where h is the height of the computed centroid tree.
If the weights are of polynomial complexity, the running time is O(n log log n).

results.problem: Weighted centroid tree construction lower bound
results.quote: Theorem 1.6. Let h \ge 3 and n \ge h+1 be integers. Then there is a tree T on at most n vertices and a class W of weight functions on V(T) such that for every w \in W, every centroid tree of (T,w) has height h, and every binary decision tree that solves T for W has height \Omega(n log h).
Theorem 1.1. Let T be a tree, w:V(T)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}, and m=w(T). Then cent(T,w) \le 2\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(T,w)-m.

Theorem 1.2. (i) For every \varepsilon>0 there is a sequence of instances (T_n,w_n) with w_n(T_n)=1, and for every centroid tree C_n of (T_n,w_n) cost_{w_n}(C_n) \ge 2\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(T_n,w_n)-1-\varepsilon.

Theorem 1.2. (ii) There is a sequence of instances (T_n,w_n), where w_n is the uniform distribution on V(T_n), and for every centroid tree C_n of (T_n,w_n) lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)}{\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)}=2.
Theorem 1.3. Let T be a tree, w:V(T)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}, and let \Delta be the maximum degree of T. Then cent(T,w) \le \left(2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta}\right)\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(T,w).

results.problem: Centroid tree approximation lower bound (bounded degree)
results.quote: Theorem 1.4. (i) There is a sequence of instances (T_n,w_n) such that T_n has maximum degree at most \Delta, and for every centroid tree C_n of (T_n,w_n) lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{\mathtt{cost}_{w_n}(C_n)}{\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)}=2-\frac{1}{2^\Delta}.

results.problem: Centroid tree approximation lower bound (bounded degree, unbounded OPT)
results.quote: Theorem 1.4. (ii) There is a sequence of instances (T_n,w_n) such that T_n has maximum degree at most \Delta, lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty, w_n(T_n)=1, and for every centroid tree C_n of (T_n,w_n) cost_{w_n}(C_n) \ge \left(2-\frac{4}{2^\Delta}\right)\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)-1.

Theorem 1.8. For every \alpha\in[\frac{1}{2},1) there is a sequence of instances (T_n,w_n) with lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathtt{OPT}(\mathcal{T}_n,w_n)=\infty, w_n(T_n)=1 and cent^\alpha(T_n,w_n) \ge \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\cdot\mathtt{OPT}(T_n,w_n)-\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}.
Theorem 1.9. Let T be an optimal STT of (T,w). Then, T is a \frac{2}{3}-centroid tree of (T,w).

Theorem 5.4. Let T be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of (T,w) in time O(n log h) \subseteq O(n log log(\sigma+n)), where h is the height of the computed centroid tree and \sigma is the spread of w.

results.bound: O(n + m \log \log \sigma) \text{ or } O(n + m \log m)
results.quote: Theorem 5.5. Let T be a tree on n vertices and w be a weight function. We can compute a centroid tree of (T,w) in time O(n + m log log \sigma) or O(n + m log m), where m is the number of vertices in T with positive weight and \sigma is the spread of w.

Theorem 5.6. Let n \in \mathbb{N} and \sigma \in \mathbb{R} with 4n \le \sigma \le 2^n. Then there is a tree T on n vertices and a class W of weight functions on V(T) with spread at most \sigma, such that every binary decision tree that solves T for W has height \Omega(n log(\frac{\sigma}{n})).
